name: Bromocriptine

lead: Bromocriptine is an ergot-derived dopamine D2 receptor agonist. Medically it is used to lower prolactin, to treat prolactin-secreting pituitary tumours, acromegaly and Parkinson's disease, and, as the quick-release Cycloset, to improve blood sugar in type 2 diabetes.

Its link to appearance is indirect. Raised prolactin can suppress testosterone, libido and fertility, so on testosterone-focused forums bromocriptine is discussed as a prolactin-lowering option, usually next to cabergoline, with the aim of restoring hormone balance and the training and body-composition gains that go with it. It is also associated with weight and glucose effects in its diabetes formulation.

paras: Under medical care it is taken by mouth, with regimens set and monitored by a prescriber through blood prolactin tests. On T Nation, members mention it as part of workups for low libido or high prolactin, often described as an older dopamine agonist that is taken daily and is less well tolerated than cabergoline.

Common effects are nausea, vomiting, headache and low blood pressure on standing. Rare effects include vasospasm with heart attack or stroke, reported mainly after postpartum use, psychotic symptoms, and pulmonary fibrosis at the high doses used for Parkinson's disease. A prolonged dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome can follow dose reduction. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia.

chain: Less prolactin-related suppression of testosterone and libido
Hormone profile that supports training and body composition
angle.text: Where raised prolactin is part of a hormonal problem, lowering it is the aim of treatment. Forum members describe it as one tool in managing that, and the diabetes formulation is linked in research to weight and glucose control.

lead: Bromocriptine is an ergoline derivative and dopamine agonist, sold as Parlodel and, in a quick-release form for type 2 diabetes, as Cycloset.[1] Sandoz discovered it in 1965 and published it in 1968; it was approved for medical use in 1975, and the FDA approved Cycloset in 2009.[1]

Its approved uses include hyperprolactinemia and its consequences (amenorrhea, infertility, hypogonadism, prolactin-secreting adenomas), acromegaly, Parkinson's disease, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and, as an adjunct to diet and exercise, type 2 diabetes.[1] Prolactinomas make up roughly 53 percent of pituitary adenomas and can cause hypogonadism, infertility and galactorrhea.[2]

In appearance-focused and testosterone-focused communities, bromocriptine is discussed as a way to lower prolactin when it is thought to be depressing libido or testosterone, so that training, recovery and body composition are not held back. T Nation threads on low testosterone and libido mention it alongside cabergoline and TRT.[3][4][5]

Medically, bromocriptine belongs to the ergoline group of dopamine agonists, an older class that has largely been supplanted for some uses by newer drugs such as cabergoline and the non-ergoline agonists.[6][7] Its main significance for appearance-minded readers is hormonal: prolactin excess suppresses the hormones that drive libido, muscle and body composition, and dopamine agonists are the standard way clinicians bring prolactin down.[8]

paras: Prescribed uses include hyperprolactinemia, prolactin-secreting pituitary tumours, acromegaly, Parkinson's disease, prevention of ovarian hyperstimulation, neuroleptic malignant syndrome and type 2 diabetes (Cycloset).[1] Off-label use for cocaine withdrawal has been reported, with poor evidence.[1] A 1974 double-blind study in 20 Parkinson's patients on conventional therapy found it gave a significant therapeutic action.[9]

Raised prolactin can lower testosterone and libido, so TRT forum members ask whether prolactin has been checked and whether bromocriptine or a related drug was tried.[4][10] Another thread describes it as an older dopamine agonist that has to be taken daily and has worse side effects than cabergoline for most people.[5]

Bromocriptine is a partial agonist at the dopamine D2 receptor and interacts with other dopamine, serotonin and adrenergic receptors.[1] For Cycloset, taking it within two hours of waking is linked to higher hypothalamic dopamine and lower glucose and insulin resistance.[1]

Prolactin is a pituitary hormone. Wikipedia's article on hyperprolactinaemia explains that excess prolactin suppresses gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which lowers FSH, LH and testosterone output; in men the result can be reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility and gynecomastia, and over time bone loss.[8] Because testosterone supports muscle, recovery and fat distribution, people interested in physique and hormone health follow this chain closely.[8]

Causes of raised prolactin include prolactin-secreting pituitary tumours, which are the most common cause overall, as well as hypothyroidism, kidney failure and many drugs, particularly dopamine-blocking antipsychotics and metoclopramide.[8] Diagnosis begins with history, medication review and laboratory testing, with MRI used when no other cause is found.[8] Dopamine agonists are first-line treatment for prolactinomas, and treatment often continues long term because prolactin tends to rise again after stopping.[8]

Cabergoline is often the first choice for prolactinomas because it binds D2 receptors more strongly, is generally better tolerated and is dosed less often.[6] Bromocriptine is often still preferred when pregnancy is possible, because there is less safety data for cabergoline.[8][6] Forum members on T Nation describe the same pattern informally, calling bromocriptine the older option with more side effects.[5]

Ergoline agonists as a class carry a higher risk of heart-valve fibrosis at the high doses used in Parkinson's disease than non-ergoline agonists, and the 2007 valvulopathy studies concerned cabergoline and pergolide; Wikipedia reports that lower prolactin-range doses were not clinically significantly associated with valve disease.[6][7]

Cycloset, a quick-release tablet, was approved by the FDA in 2009 as an adjunct to diet and exercise in type 2 diabetes.[1] Wikipedia reports that taken within two hours of waking it is associated with higher hypothalamic dopamine, lower hepatic glucose production, better insulin resistance and some weight loss.[1] This formulation is the main place where bromocriptine intersects with body-composition outcomes in the clinical literature.

Bromocriptine has been used to suppress milk production after childbirth. A 2014 review could not exclude a causal link with serious cardiovascular, neurological or psychiatric events, estimating overall incidence at 0.005 to 0.04 percent; regulators including the European Medicines Agency's CMDh endorsed restricted use and extra precautions.[1]

sections.h: Dopamine agonist withdrawal and impulse control
paras: After long-term use, dose reduction or discontinuation of dopamine agonists can produce a withdrawal syndrome with anxiety, panic, depression, fatigue, nausea and cravings; in some people it is protracted and lasts months or years.[7] Dopamine agonists as a class have also been linked to impulse control disorders such as compulsive gambling, hypersexuality, shopping and binge eating.[7]

Common effects are nausea, orthostatic hypotension, headache and vomiting. Rare effects include vasospasm with serious cardiovascular events reported postpartum, psychotic symptoms, and pulmonary fibrosis at high Parkinson's-range doses. Dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome can follow reduction or discontinuation.[1]

Human trials of bromocriptine cover Parkinson's disease, prolactin disorders, acromegaly and dystonia. A 1974 randomized double-blind study in 20 Parkinson's patients found a significant therapeutic action, with neurological deficits improving almost 20 percent in severely disabled patients and about 10 percent in mildly affected ones.[9] Reviews of pituitary adenomas describe dopamine agonists in prolactinoma management.[2] No published trial has tested it for cosmetic or physique goals.

Sandoz scientists discovered bromocriptine in 1965; the patent (US 3,752,814, '2-Bromo-alpha-ergocryptine') names E. Flückiger and A. Hofmann as inventors and describes making it by brominating ergocryptine.[1] It was published and patented in 1968, approved for medical use in 1975 and first marketed as Parlodel.[1] Wikipedia's dopamine agonist article says bromocriptine came into wide use in Parkinson's disease from 1974, when its benefit was recognised, and that combining agonists with levodopa could cut the levodopa dose by 20 to 30 percent.[7] Cabergoline followed, with FDA approval on 23 December 1996.[6] The FDA approved Cycloset in 2009.[1]

Oral bioavailability is about 28 percent, metabolism is extensive in the liver, the elimination half-life is 12 to 14 hours, and about 85 percent is excreted in bile.[1] It is a partial D2 agonist that also interacts with D3, serotonin and adrenergic receptors.[1]
It is prescription-only in Australia (Schedule 4), Canada, the UK and the US.[1] On T Nation it appears in discussions of low libido, prolactin and TRT.[3][4][5][10]

timeline.event: Bromocriptine comes into wide use for Parkinson's disease; a double-blind study of 20 patients is published.[9][7]
Approved for medical use as Parlodel.[1]
FDA approves cabergoline, which later becomes first-line for many prolactin disorders.[6]
Studies link cabergoline and pergolide to heart-valve disease; pergolide leaves the US market.[6]
FDA approves quick-release Cycloset for type 2 diabetes.[1]
Review of postpartum use cannot exclude a link to rare serious events; EU regulators restrict use.[1]
